One continuous 10-second infinity zoom-out shot for a bright, hyper-glossy Y2K music video, in which the entire visible world spins slowly and continuously clockwise inside the frame from the very first frame to the very last, completing exactly one full revolution. The camera never cuts. It pulls backward the whole time while the world turns: horizons tilt, walls rotate past, floors climb the frame edges. Each scene is revealed to be a live image nested inside an object in the next scene. Every nested hand-off is purely geometric — the ongoing scene stays fully solid and opaque while its container simply grows in around it as the camera pulls back; nothing ever fades, dissolves, or turns transparent. The final scene is the same city street as the opening, arriving right-side-up again as the revolution completes, closing a perfect loop.

ACTIVE REFERENCES 
<<<image_1>>> is the STREET MAN character reference — Y2K man: yellow striped beanie, yellow open-mesh tee over white long-sleeve, chunky silver chains with a square pendant, white bead bracelet, black jorts with a huge silver ball chain, yellow-black-white sneakers. <<<image_2>>> is the BATH GIRL character reference — Y2K girl: long black hair with wispy bangs, hot-pink halter crop top with a white satin bow, silver star belly chain, star necklace, pink bead bracelet. Identical to this reference (in the tub, visible waist-up above the foam). 
<<<image_3>>> is the ARCADE BOY character reference — Y2K boy: backwards royal-blue cap over dark curls, thin mustache, blue mesh V-neck jersey over white tee, shell necklace, stud earrings, baggy washed denim, blue-white sneakers. Identical to this reference. 
<<<image_4>>> is the BARBER GIRL character reference — Y2K girl: long braids with lime-green strands, lime-green off-shoulder long-sleeve crop top, gold bangles and earrings, gold plate necklace, lime belt with a jeweled buckle and a lime bandana at her hip, grey baggy pants, lime fuzzy leg warmers, green-and-white nails. Identical to this reference. 
<<<image_5>>> is the STREET location reference — sunlit London-style street: red, yellow and teal shopfronts, brick uppers, blue sky, a red barbershop storefront with a chrome barber pole at frame left. Controls scene 1 and scene 5. All existing signage stays exactly as in the reference; no new readable text ever appears anywhere in the video.

TEXT-DEFINED LOCATIONS (no image references — build these from description, in the same bright Y2K world) 
BATHROOM (scene 2): a vivid hot-pink glossy-tiled bathroom with turquoise trim, a white bathtub crowned with dense turquoise foam, gold vintage fixtures, colorful bottles on a pink shelf, and a gold-framed picture hanging on the tiled wall directly above the tub — the frame where the live street scene lives. 
ARCADE (scene 3): a dark neon arcade with rows of decorated cabinets, curved glowing CRT screens, red joysticks and colorful buttons, pink and green neon tubes glowing against the dark — the foreground cabinet's CRT is where the live bathroom scene plays. 
BARBERSHOP (scene 4): a bright modern barbershop with a black-and-white checkerboard floor, red leather barber chairs, bulb-lit mirrors, shelves of colorful product bottles, a chrome-and-glass front looking onto the street, a spinning barber pole visible outside, and a slim wall-mounted flatscreen TV high on the wall — the TV where the live arcade scene plays.

First frame, right-side-up: the man from <<<image_1>>> stands center frame on the sunlit street from <<<image_5>>>, facing camera, mid-gesture with one hand raised, framed waist-up, colorful shopfronts running deep behind him. In the very first second the whole street already begins to tilt clockwise in frame — the horizon visibly rotating, buildings starting to lean. FORMAT MODE 
16:9 horizontal, single continuous take, 10 seconds.

OPTICS 
84° diagonal field of view, classic wide rectilinear character. Lens locked for the whole shot; all zoom-out is physical camera pull-back, no focal-length drift, no fisheye.

CAMERA

A one-take ride shot: exactly one single continuous 8-second shot in 16:9, filmed by one flying camera that is PHYSICALLY MOVING THROUGH THE AIR during every single second of the video — it never stands still, never hovers in place, never becomes a static tripod shot. There is no editing — no cuts, no dissolves, no transitions, no shot changes of any kind. A coaster car full of five euphoric friends races through the drop and bends of a red roller coaster in a sunlit vintage fairground, while the flying camera travels one big smooth circle AROUND the ride, keeping the car in frame every moment from first frame to last.

ACTIVE REFERENCES

Controls the environment, rides, palette and light; existing stall signage stays exactly as in the reference, soft and unreadable — no new readable text appears anywhere.

THE RIDERS (text-defined, consistent for the whole shot) 
Five friends in their twenties packed into one coaster car, two rows: front row — a laughing young woman with flying auburn hair and sunglasses in a navy jacket, and a dark-haired young woman in a knit sweater; back row — a tall young man in a dark suit jacket with both arms raised high, a blond young man mid-scream, and a red-haired young woman laughing with her head tipped back. All casual-smart, all radiating uncontainable joy.

FIRST FRAME AND SPATIAL BLOCKING 
First frame: the camera is already flying sideways through the air — the fairground visibly sliding across the frame with parallax from the very first frame — with the red coaster structure at center, the packed car just tipping over its first crest, five riders clearly visible; the Ferris wheel, carousel, striped stalls and bunting surround the coaster on all sides.

OPTICS 
35° natural wide cinematic rendering, crisp and rectilinear, at a fixed focal length — no zooming in or out; every change of framing comes from the camera physically flying closer, farther, or around.

CAMERA — CONSTANT FLIGHT 
For all 8 seconds the camera is an FPV drone in continuous flight along one unbroken counter-clockwise circular path around the roller coaster structure, at rider height, moving fast enough that the background NEVER stops sliding: in every single frame of the video, the Ferris wheel, carousel, stalls, bunting and sky are visibly traveling across the frame with strong parallax — this continuous background motion is the proof that the camera is always flying. The circle's radius breathes as it flies — sweeping closer as the car drops toward the camera's side of the structure, arcing wider as the car banks away — but the flight never stops, never pauses, never reverses, never hovers, and never jumps. Because the camera keeps traveling around the ride while the car races through drops and bends inside the circle, their relative angle changes constantly: the riders are seen head-on, then in profile, then from behind, then in profile again, all within the one unbroken lap. Real coaster physics on every body: weightless float at the crest, violent upward hair and clothing whip through the drop, unified sideways lean through the banks, natural bounce on the rise; hands grip the safety bar except when raised. The camera flies with real aerial momentum — one continuous banked circular flight with gentle radius breathing, spatially consistent with the fairground's geometry, never clipping through the coaster structure, riders or scenery, and never coming to rest. Background parallax and motion blur match the true relative speed between the flying camera and the racing car at every moment; there is no frame in the video where the background is stationary. Constant real-time speed throughout, no slow motion anywhere.

LIGHTING 
Bright golden afternoon sun in a deep blue sky with scattered white clouds: the sun travels around the frame as the camera flies its lap — flaring into the lens on one side of the circle, backlighting flying hair on the opposite side — faces lit by open-sky bounce, the fairground saturated and sunlit in every direction. Natural lens flares from the real sun only.

AUDIO 
Roaring wind rush that never dies down — the constant airflow of a camera in flight; the rhythmic clatter of coaster wheels swelling and softening as the flying camera nears and recedes from the track; five voices screaming, whooping and laughing in real bursts; the fairground rotating through the soundfield — carousel organ, crowd murmur, a ride bell — panning continuously with the camera's lap; a shared burst of breathless laughter as the car races toward the lens at the end. No dialogue lines, no narration, no music track.

STYLE 
Hyper-realistic FPV-drone cinematography with premium commercial polish: crisp sunlit image, saturated fairground palette of reds, golds and sky blue, one masterful continuous flight line graded like a feel-good summer ad, every frame bursting with motion and joy.

QUALITY 
Stable rendering at constant real speed: all five riders stay consistent in identity, seating order and clothing for the whole shot, faces readable whenever they face the camera; no ghosting, no duplicated limbs, no warping of the track, car or Ferris wheel as the camera flies around them; motion blur natural to the relative speeds, resolving sharp in the final head-on frames.

This video is one single continuous take filmed by a camera in uninterrupted flight: one flying camera, one unbroken counter-clockwise circular movement around the roller coaster, zero cuts, zero dissolves, zero transitions, zero shot changes, and ZERO static frames — the background shows visible parallax motion in every frame of the video, and the camera never hovers, never parks, never locks onto a fixed position. The coaster car with its five riders is visible in every frame from first to last. Exactly five riders appear, matching the text descriptions in identity, seating and wardrobe throughout; no one leaves or enters the car; background fairground visitors stay distant and soft. The fairground matches <<<image_1>>> throughout, its signage unchanged and unreadable, with no new text anywhere. The ride flows crest → drop → banked turn → far bend → rise in one unbroken run. Every second plays at normal real-time speed with no slow motion.

SCENE CONTEXT 
One continuous 10s anime action shot in 16:9 with no cuts: inside the cargo hold of a flying plane, a SWAT cat fights a rogue cat through a hold full of breakable cargo and wins — then dives backward out of the open cargo ramp into the night, falling ON HIS BACK framed by a rigid body-mounted snorricam, tumbling crates falling through the sky around him, snaps his night-vision goggles down over his eyes, and as the camera makes a small orbit around his head it flies INTO a goggle lens — ending inside his point of view: an anime night city far below in green night-vision, with ANOTHER AIRPLANE sweeping past through the green view. The camera is restless and handheld through the fight, rigid body-locked in the fall, and finishes inside his eyes. Both cats act with small, expressive anime emotions — determination, fury, effort, surprise — always readable, never mugging. Anime style, ferocious pace, small grounded visual effects on every impact, no dialogue.

ACTIVE REFERENCES 
<<<image_1>>> is the HERO, the SWAT CAT — an anthropomorphic grey tabby cat with dark stripes, sharp yellow eyes and white muzzle, in a navy tactical uniform with rolled sleeves, a black plate carrier with radio, black gloves, knee pads, boots, and a black helmet mounting a four-lens night-vision device flipped UP; striped tail. Identical to this reference throughout. His acting: focused professional determination — narrowed eyes, ears forward and controlled — with small honest beats breaking through: a wince of effort on the hardest block, a grim set of the jaw as he finishes the fight, calm resolve smoothing his face in the freefall. 
<<<image_2>>> is the VILLAIN, the ROGUE CAT — an anthropomorphic Siamese cat with a dark mask-like face, ice-blue eyes and a scar across the muzzle, in torn black-and-grey tactical gear: a ragged sleeveless shirt, patched plate carrier, battered helmet with a four-lens night-vision device where one lens is cracked and dead, fingerless gloves, boots; brown tail. Identical to this reference throughout. His acting: snarling feral aggression — bared teeth, ears pinned flat, pupils slitted — cracking into one wide-eyed flash of surprise when his knife arm is caught, and ending dazed and glaring weakly from under the spilled cargo. 
<<<image_3>>> is the LOCATION — the cargo hold of a large aircraft: a long ribbed vaulted ceiling with strip lights, cream paneled walls with tie-down hatches, rows of floor rails studded with yellow-and-red cargo clamps, a ladder against the right wall, and the hold opening at its far end into darkness — the open rear cargo ramp, night sky beyond. Identical to this reference in geometry and light — and dressed with cargo: stacks of olive wooden crates and steel cases strapped along both walls, a netted pallet of duffel bags and boxes mid-hold, a small strapped-down quad bike near the left wall, a cluster of steel fuel drums by the ladder, loose straps and a hanging cargo hook swaying with the engine drone.

FIRST FRAME AND SPATIAL BLOCKING 
First frame: mid-fight, mid-swing — the SWAT cat and the rogue cat already locked in close combat at the center of the cargo hold, the rogue's teeth bared and the SWAT cat's eyes narrowed in focus, crate stacks and the netted pallet around them, the strapped quad bike at the left wall, fuel drums by the ladder, the open dark ramp yawning at the far end behind them, strip lights streaking overhead, the handheld camera already lunging with the action. No calm before it; the video opens inside the violence.

OPTICS 
Anime cinematic rendering, crisp character line work over painted backgrounds; a wide 65° feel in the hold, tightening to an intimate 50° body-locked framing in the snorricam. No zooms — every framing change comes from camera movement or the rig.

CAMERA — THREE JOINED MOVEMENTS, ONE UNBROKEN TAKE 
[0-4.5s] THE FIGHT — restless handheld: the camera never settles for a single beat — lunging with strikes, whipping with reversals, ducking under a kick, shoving in close on impacts and tearing back out, weaving between crate stacks as the fighters crash through them, always breathing, always shaking with the hits, strip lights smearing overhead, the open ramp swinging in and out of frame. It is never stable, never on a tripod, never still. 
[4.5-5s] THE DIVE TRANSITION: as the SWAT cat sprints for the ramp and launches himself backward off its edge into the dark, the camera dives after him and LOCKS ON — becoming a rigid snorricam mounted to his chest harness.

He is rock-solid in frame; everything else falls and turns. 
[8.5-10s] THE ORBIT INTO THE GOGGLES: still falling on his back, he reaches up and snaps the four-lens night-vision device DOWN over his eyes and rolls his body over to face the earth — the camera releasing from the rig into one small smooth orbit around his helmet, arcing from his profile to head-on, and then flying forward INTO the glowing green glass of a goggle lens — the lens filling the frame until the image becomes his POV: the anime night city sprawling far below in green night-vision — phosphor-green monochrome, glowing window grids, streets like bright veins, soft bloom on every light, a hint of scanline and vignette at the edges, the horizon tilting gently with his fall — and cutting across the green view BELOW him, another airplane sweeps past: a large aircraft crossing left to right beneath his fall, its engines blooming as hot green flares in the night-vision, its navigation lights pulsing bright, a faint green contrail shearing behind it as it thunders across the city glow and carries on. 0-1.5s — THE EXCHANGE: the rogue cat slashes with a combat knife in fast anime combos, snarling with bared teeth, ears pinned flat — the blade scrapes the SWAT cat's forearm guard in a thin trail of orange sparks, the SWAT cat's face tightening in a small wince of effort before his eyes narrow harder; he weaves and answers with two sharp jabs that knock the rogue back INTO a crate stack — the top crate bursting apart in a spray of splinters and spilling packed gear across the floor rails, a small dust burst blooming on the impact. 
1.5-3s — THE TURN: the rogue lunges too hard, fury wide in his ice-blue eyes — the SWAT cat catches the knife arm, and for one held drawing the rogue's snarl cracks into wide-eyed surprise — the SWAT cat twists the arm into a lock and slams him across the strapped quad bike, the machine rocking hard against its straps, a mirror snapping off and skittering away; the knife flies loose and clangs off a fuel drum with a bright spark ping; a knee to the gut folds the rogue, a spinning elbow cracks across his helmet — the dead lens shattering in a tiny burst of glass glitter. 
3-4.5s — THE FINISH: one clean anime-fast roundhouse sends the rogue cat crashing through the netted pallet — bags and boxes avalanching down over him in a whump of dust, leaving him tangled and limp under the spilled cargo, glaring weakly through half-lidded dazed eyes, beaten; the SWAT cat holds one breath in a strong stepped pose, ears flat, jaw set in a grim beat of resolve — loose papers and packing straw still fluttering down through the air around him — then his ears swivel toward the ramp, and he turns and SPRINTS for it, vaulting a fallen crate.

Final frame: the green city and the crossing plane through his eyes.

Every impact in the fight carries a small physical effect and nothing larger: thin orange spark trails where blade meets metal, brief spark pings off drums and rails, dust bursts and splinter sprays from breaking crates, a glitter of glass from the shattering lens, packing straw and papers drifting after the pallet crash, faint anime impact flashes lasting a single frame on the hardest hits. The backward leap off the ramp carries his sprint momentum into true freefall; the dislodged crates and bag fall with him at naturally diverging rates, tumbling with authentic aerodynamics; in the snorricam his body is fixed relative to camera while wind physics rip at fur, straps and whiskers and the world rotates with authentic aerial parallax; the parachute stays packed on his back — it never opens in this video. The goggle snap-down is a crisp mechanical action. The second airplane in the POV flies a straight, level crossing path far below him with true aircraft speed and perspective, its contrail shearing naturally. Constant real-time speed throughout — no slow motion anywhere; the fight's speed lives in anime timing, smears and impact frames.

In the hold: cool strip-light fluorescence from the vaulted ceiling, hard small shadows under the fighters, dust from the breaking crates catching the light in drifting motes, the far ramp a rectangle of pure night; impact beats punctuated by quick single-frame anime flashes. In the fall: cold moonlight rimming his fur, helmet and the tumbling cargo against deep blue night, city glow washing faintly from below, his face readable in every frame. Both cats carry small readable emotions throughout — always expressive, never exaggerated mugging. The SWAT cat wins the fight decisively; the rogue cat ends beaten, buried under the spilled pallet cargo, alive, and never reappears after the jump. Destruction is confined to cargo and props — the hero's plane is never damaged and keeps flying. STAY COOL — 20-second black-and-violet poster-motion edit starring the user.

INPUT
One clear photo of one person: the user, or someone who agreed to it. No public figures, no children. That person is the only star. Keep their face and identity exactly the same in every shot. Never mix in a second person.

OUTPUT
- 20.000 s, 400 frames, 1440×1080 (4:3), 20 fps, H.264 + AAC.
- Keep the reference video's soundtrack exactly as it is. It is an original, license-free track made for this preset.
- Never use the audio of the generations. Never add or swap music.
- Cut everything on its 120 BPM grid: 1 beat = 10 frames, 1 bar = 40 frames, felt half-time.

LOOK
- Footage treatment: high-contrast halftone duotone in black → violet.
 - Shadows #0B0612. Mids #7B3BA9. Light lilac #D9B8EC only on faces and skin.
 - Fine 5 px halftone dots, crisp, strong contrast.
- Cut-outs: the person is cut out of every shot, with a thin 3 px lilac rim along the cut-out edge. The studio wall is never visible.
 - Every panel, window and card is a cut-out on a flat black (#0B0612) or violet (#7B3BA9) field.
 - Fields alternate black / violet. In the drop they flip on every cut.
 - A deep-violet (#3A1757) halftone-dot floor sits at the bottom of the frame.
- One orchid disc (#CB5AE0) runs through the whole edit:
 - it is born as a single dot;
 - it becomes the O of the words, a circle window onto the face, a halo behind the head, a hub, then a full flood.
 - Orchid is used ONLY for the disc.
- The edit ends on one pale flash frame (#F8ECFB). Hard cut. No titles, no end card, no logo.

TYPE
- Two faces only:
 - a condensed black grotesk in CAPS for the big words;
 - a high-contrast didone italic in lowercase for the small words.
- Text colour: paper #EBD6F1 or lilac #AD69CD.
- Words slam in on the beat and hold; letters can act as windows into the footage.
- The person may pass in front of the words, but every word must stay readable.
- Fixed copy, in this order, exactly: SLOW down · NO · NO RUSH · I SET THE pace · ON MY own time · every angle · NOTHING to prove · I DON'T chase · STILL me · EYES on me · KEEP up · YOUR MOVE · stay COOL.
- Never change, translate or add words. Never put the user's own text on screen.

- an identity HERO still from the photo;
- a full-body LOOK still with a locked outfit: plain white fitted top, open black jacket, black straight trousers, black boots, no logos;
- everything on a plain very light warm-grey seamless studio cyclorama, so the cut-outs come out clean.

Make a 20-second golden-hour sport aura edit, 16:9, for any sport the user names (default: rowing, double scull). Look: shot straight into a low sun at sunrise or sunset. Strong backlight and lens flares, deep teal sky and shadows against warm gold highlights, halation. Vintage ultra-wide lens: barrel distortion, soft corners, chromatic fringing, vignette, film grain, gate weave. The sport's element (water spray, dust, snow, sand) flies through the backlight and glows gold.

Camera: moving in every shot. FPV dives and skims, orbits, crash zooms, fast tracking at ground or water level, handheld jolts. Slow motion on the impacts and on the aura moments.

Beats, in order:
1. Intro: athlete B slowly turns his head and stares into the lens, fast push-in, cut to black.
2. Drop: the gear slams into the element and blasts golden spray at the lens, white flash.
3. Fast cuts on the beat: hands on the grip, the drive, both athletes at full effort, an FPV dive over the place, a rush past, a high aerial.
4. A tape-stop: the action slows to a black-and-white freeze.
5. Break: athlete A glances into the lens with a slight confident smile, colour returns, then a flash montage.
6. Second drop: the two lift their gear as a silhouette against the sun.
7. An eighth-note run with black-and-white step-print inserts.
8. The two bump fists: freeze and flash on the touch.
9. They move away into the sun, the light blooms, fade to black.

Edit: cut on a 125 BPM grid. Speed ramps with motion blur, zoom punches, camera jolts, RGB split, whip, spin and zoom-through transitions. Music: an original dark phonk-style track (cowbell melody, distorted 808, hard claps) with its hits on the cuts.

No text, captions, logos or watermark. No real people unless the user supplies them. Nobody else in the frame.

Read this reference in Stage 2 for source normalization and in Stage 7 for final
delivery. Run all commands through `sandbox_exec`. Every finalization group must
download inputs, process, verify, and PUT passing files in one self-contained
call because sandbox files are ephemeral.

## Source probe normalization

Download only the trusted hosted source URL, following HTTPS redirects only and
limiting it to 500 MiB. Probe with:

```bash
curl --fail --location --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' --retry 2 --max-filesize 524288000 --output source.mp4 "$SOURCE_URL"
ffprobe -v error -show_streams -show_format -of json -- source.mp4
```

Normalize the JSON deterministically:

1. Select the primary non-cover-art video stream: prefer
 `disposition.default=1`, otherwise the first video stream whose
 `disposition.attached_pic` is not `1`.

 primary video stream's duration. Reject missing/non-finite duration and any
 result outside 4.0-30.0 seconds.

 default `1:1`. Display aspect is `(coded_width * SAR) / coded_height`; invert
 it after normalized 90° or 270° rotation from side data or `tags.rotate`.

 only for duration tolerance.

# Recreate mode — Ad Multiplier Recreate

Recreate re-shoots one supplied 4-30 second source ad as new footage for
another market, audience, spoken language, cast, product, or setting, while the
backend keeps the source's structure: its beats, order, timing, pacing, aspect
ratio, and capture style. Each output is one `ad_multiplier_v2` generation.
The same model can also regenerate only the source's hook, its CTA, or both,
and stitch them back in; see [Hook or CTA only](#hook-or-cta-only).

The backend owns the creative work and every decision. For every job it
analyzes the source, reads the prompt and the images, decides the language,
product, cast, image roles, audio, and setting from them, writes the generation
prompt, renders `ceil(source duration)` seconds at the source aspect ratio (an
unlisted ratio such as 4:5 renders at the nearest supported one), and restores
the source audio when it keeps it. Therefore, in this mode:

# Kids · Talking Characters (`talking_characters: true`)

Read this only for a Kids run whose sound alternates between the narrator and the cast.
Every other run ignores this file.

Odd blocks are **narration**: the external narrator speaks and every character keeps
their mouth closed. Even blocks are **dialogue**: at most two named characters speak
inside the generated `minimax_h3` clip. Duration stays unchanged:
`blocks = ceil(requested_seconds / 10)` and the alternation continues across all blocks.

The flag changes the whole script, not only the prompts:

- Keep one chronological story. Each dialogue block must be caused by the narration
 before it and set up the narration after it. A dialogue block that can move elsewhere
 without breaking the story must be rewritten.
- Narration blocks use 17–21 words per 10 seconds. Dialogue blocks use 16–22 words total
 across all speakers so turn-taking does not create long dead air.
- A dialogue block names at most two speaking characters. Give each one turn, two only
 when essential. Never introduce knowledge or a character before the story has shown it.
- The clip's native voices are accepted for dialogue blocks. Character timbre may vary;
 keep visual identity, wardrobe, palette, and the shared delivery direction stable.
- Narration blocks receive normal fixed-window `narration` takes. Dialogue blocks use the
 clip's own full-length audio: extract it, normalize it to −16 LUFS, and pass it to the
 assembler as that block's `voiceNN.wav`. Never center or replace dialogue audio because
 it must stay locked to the lips.
- SONG MODE and Talking Characters are mutually exclusive in one video. An explicit song
 request wins. `channel_dna.talking_characters` describes this video only and does not
 lock the next episode.
- All other Kids rules remain: four cuts, narrator/character/viewer interplay, default
 wordless music bed, the same style key, and the same asset roster.

In `script_manifest.json`, set top-level `talking_characters:true` and alternate
`block_kind:"narration"|"dialogue"` starting with narration. For a dialogue block,
`vo_line` is the combined spoken text in playback order and `speakers` lists its one or
two ordered speaker names; keep the speaker-attributed lines in the authored script. The
motion validator enforces the flag, alternation, word bands, and speaker count.

## Core principle

**Cinematic realism is built from restraint, not spectacle.** Every prompt enforces five grounding pillars that prevent Seedance from drifting into the over-animated, floaty, AI-looking failure modes that plague text-to-video output.

The five pillars:

1. **Body weight & physics** — actors have mass; movement has friction, momentum, and contact force.
2. **Environmental force** — wind, water, gravity, fabric, and surface texture push back on the actor.
3. **Emotional restraint** — micro-expressions, held beats, breath. No exaggerated facial telegraphing.
4. **Camera as observer** — the lens has its own physical presence (weight, breathing, drift). Not a drone, not a god.
5. **Continuity anchors** — lighting direction, wardrobe, time-of-day, and prop position carry across shots.

A prompt that drops any pillar produces "AI cinema" — technically a video, structurally a tell.

## The grounded cinematic prompt structure

Seedance 2.0 prompts for cinematic film follow this six-block order. The order is load-bearing — Seedance weights the earliest blocks most heavily for compositional decisions, and the later blocks for motion and audio.

[STYLE & MOOD]
[SHOT DIRECTION]
[ACTOR BEHAVIOR]
[ENVIRONMENTAL FORCE]
[CAMERA BEHAVIOR]
[AUDIO]

## Foundational Thinking Models

These models sharpen your strategy and help you solve the right problems.

### First Principles
Break problems down to basic truths and build solutions from there. Instead of copying competitors, ask "why" repeatedly to find root causes. Use the 5 Whys technique to tunnel down to what really matters.

**Marketing application**: Don't assume you need content marketing because competitors do. Ask why you need it, what problem it solves, and whether there's a better solution.

### Jobs to Be Done
People don't buy products—they "hire" them to get a job done. Focus on the outcome customers want, not features.

**Marketing application**: A drill buyer doesn't want a drill—they want a hole. Frame your product around the job it accomplishes, not its specifications.

### Circle of Competence
Know what you're good at and stay within it. Venture outside only with proper learning or expert help.

**Marketing application**: Don't chase every channel. Double down where you have genuine expertise and competitive advantage.

### Inversion
Instead of asking "How do I succeed?", ask "What would guarantee failure?" Then avoid those things.

**Marketing application**: List everything that would make your campaign fail—confusing messaging, wrong audience, slow landing page—then systematically prevent each.

### Occam's Razor
The simplest explanation is usually correct. Avoid overcomplicating strategies or attributing results to complex causes when simple ones suffice.

**Marketing application**: If conversions dropped, check the obvious first (broken form, page speed) before assuming complex attribution issues.

### Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)

This skill provides the five-pillar language system for constructing video prompts with
cinematic precision. Apply it to any video generation task — atmosphere shots, product reveals,

The core principle: **the model understands physics, geometry, sequence, and constraint —

temporal sequence, or hard rule.

## The Five Pillars

### 1. Camera Contract
State the camera's behavior as a hard rule before describing anything else.
The model treats the camera as a character — define it or it will improvise.

Examples:
- "Static locked-off camera. Zero movement. No pan, no zoom, no dolly, no shake."
- "Slow push-in only — 10% scale change over the full duration."
- "Single handheld drift, slight organic sway, no cuts."

Always reinforce camera rules in the negative prompt as well.

Give every moving element a speed reference from the physical world, not an adjective.

- "like smoke through a cathedral at dawn"

A transformation prompt has two jobs that pull against each other: **lock** everything that makes

# Copywriting

You are an expert conversion copywriter. Your goal is to write marketing copy that is clear, compelling, and drives action.

## Before Writing

**Check for product marketing context first:**
If `.agents/product-marketing-context.md` exists (or `.AI Director/product-marketing-context.md` in older setups), read it before asking questions. Use that context and only ask for information not already covered or specific to this task.

- Who is the ideal customer?
- What problem are they trying to solve?
- What objections or hesitations do they have?

### 3. Product/Offer
- What are you selling or offering?
- What makes it different from alternatives?
- What's the key transformation or outcome?
- Any proof points (numbers, testimonials, case studies)?

### 4. Context
- Where is traffic coming from? (ads, organic, email)
- What do visitors already know before arriving?

---

## Copywriting Principles

### Clarity Over Cleverness
If you have to choose between clear and creative, choose clear.

### Benefits Over Features
Features: What it does. Benefits: What that means for the customer.

### Specificity Over Vagueness
- Vague: "Save time on your workflow"
- Specific: "Cut your weekly reporting from 4 hours to 15 minutes"

### Customer Language Over Company Language
Use words your customers use. Mirror voice-of-customer from reviews, interviews, support tickets.

### One Idea Per Section
Each section should advance one argument. Build a logical flow down the page.

---

## Writing Style Rules

### Core Principles

1. **Simple over complex** — "Use" not "utilize," "help" not "facilitate"
2. **Specific over vague** — Avoid "streamline," "optimize," "innovative"
3. **Active over passive** — "We generate reports" not "Reports are generated"
4. **Confident over qualified** — Remove "almost," "very," "really"
5. **Show over tell** — Describe the outcome instead of using adverbs
6. **Honest over sensational** — Fabricated statistics or testimonials erode trust and create legal liability

### Quick Quality Check

- Jargon that could confuse outsiders?
- Sentences trying to do too much?
- Passive voice constructions?
- Exclamation points? (remove them)
- Marketing buzzwords without substance?

For thorough line-by-line review, use the **copy-editing** skill after your draft.

Based on comprehensive analysis of top-performing Seedance 2.0 prompts, every prompt must follow these **5 Operational Laws**:

1. **Temporal Anchoring (Timeline Partitioning):** Never write open-ended instructions. Every visual sequence must be broken down by exact seconds (e.g., `(0:00-0:02)` or `0–3 sec`) to coordinate complex movements.

# Prompt Engineering Expert

Use this skill to make prompts clearer, more reliable, easier to evaluate, and better matched to the model, task, tools, and operating context.

## Workflow

1. Identify the prompt's job: task, audience, model or agent context, available tools, inputs, output consumers, and failure cost.
2. Diagnose weaknesses before rewriting: ambiguity, missing context, conflicting instructions, brittle examples, unsafe scope, untestable success criteria, output format gaps, or token bloat.
3. Choose the lightest effective technique: direct instructions first; add roles, examples, structured tags, staged reasoning, tool-use guidance, or prompt chaining only when they solve a concrete issue.
4. Produce an improved prompt or instruction set with enough surrounding explanation for the user to evaluate the tradeoffs.
5. Define validation: expected behaviors, edge cases, regression cases, and success criteria.

## Response Pattern

For prompt reviews, prefer this structure:

- **Diagnosis**: the highest-impact issues, ordered by severity.
- **Revision**: a ready-to-use improved prompt.
- **Why It Works**: concise rationale for major changes.
- **Tests**: representative cases the user should run.

- Ask for missing high-risk constraints only if they cannot be reasonably assumed.
- Otherwise state assumptions and draft the prompt.
- Include variables/placeholders when the prompt should be reusable.
- Include a short evaluation checklist.

- Make the task objective explicit.
- Give only the context needed to perform the task.
- State non-negotiable constraints separately from preferences.
- Specify the expected output format when downstream use matters.
- Use examples to teach patterns, not to smuggle one-off answers.
- Avoid hidden contradictions between role, task, constraints, and format.

Common skeletons — mix, modify, or throw out as needed:

```
ABABCB Verse/Chorus/Verse/Chorus/Bridge/Chorus (most pop/rock)

ABAB Verse/Chorus alternating (simple, direct)

```

The six building blocks:
- Intro — set the mood, pull the listener in
- Verse — the story, the details, the world-building
- Pre-Chorus — optional tension ramp before the payoff
- Chorus — the emotional core, the part people remember
- Bridge — a detour, a shift in perspective or key
- Outro — the farewell, can echo or subvert the rest

that evolves. Structure serves the emotion, not the other way around.

RHYME TYPES (from tight to loose):
- Perfect: lean/mean
- Family: crate/braid
- Assonance: had/glass (same vowels, different endings)
- Consonance: scene/when (different vowels, similar endings)
- Near/slant: enough to suggest connection without locking it down

Mix them. All perfect rhymes can sound like a nursery rhyme.
All slant rhymes can sound lazy. The blend is where it lives.

INTERNAL RHYME: Rhyming within a line, not just at the ends.
 "We pruned the lies from bleeding trees / Distilled the storm
 from entropy" — "lies/flies," "trees/entropy" create internal echoes.

METER: The rhythm of stressed vs unstressed syllables.
- Matching syllable counts between parallel lines helps singability
- The STRESSED syllables matter more than total count

- Intentionally breaking meter can create emphasis or surprise

strip back to vulnerability. Works for ballads, epics, anthems.

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE once triggered. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only when user says "stop caveman" or "normal mode".

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK.
